subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is difficult for me to interpret my hon. friend's point of view, but I will say this, that when the provinces were not in a position to obtain funds on their own account there was only one source from which they could get assistance to carry them through and that was the federal treasury. However, I leave the point there.
Let me now refer again to some of the remarks of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. He spoke of the tremendous dead weight of the national and international debt and showed how that would have to be adjusted before we could approach more prosperous times. To a certain extent I am in sympathy with that view; yet, when I ask myself what hon. gentlemen opposite have done in that regard, I find that they have done exactly the opposite of what we have been told they ought to do. In fact, they have not only increased the debt by enormous sums, but they have done something for which I cannot forgive them. When they wanted money recently they offered the highest rate of interest ever known in the history of this dominion, and that rate of interest on federal bonds reflected itself in all other classes of bonds in Canada. We find, therefore, that this action of the government in offering 51 per cent interest on gilt edged securities of the federal treasury meant the adding of millions upon millions of dollars to public debts in this dominion; because the moment the federal government issued bonds at 5i per cent our provincial government had to pay 6 and 6| per cent on money it wished to borrow. The securities of the city of Winnipeg are second to those of no other city in Canada; yet in Winnipeg they had to pay 6f per cent before they could borrow money. In other words, they had to increase the amount of interest charges by approximately 50 per cent before the banks would lend them money.
Very commendable as have been certain aspects of the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, it seems to me that both hon. gentlemen who have spoken today have approached the budget statement in exactly the same way as a director or a financier would look upon a bank statement. But may I point out that in government there is something more than finance; there is more than that in running the affairs of a country. There are in this country ten million human beings, besides the financial interests of Canada, and when the Minister of Trade and Commerce says that we should study our social problems I would add that in my humble judgment the needs and desires and the well being of the ten million inhabitants of Can-

The Budget-Mr. Heaps
ada have a prior claim over the financial interests of the dominion.
I wish to offer a few words of comment on the budget statement made to this house by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes). Last year the house was treated to what was commonly called a real budget. This year no such description has been used of the budget, but the result of the first real budget we had in 1931 is that we find ourselves now with a deficit of $55,000,000; and in order to make that deficit as low as it was the government found it necessary to cut the estimates by $55,000,000. Now bon. gentlemen opposite come along requesting great increases in taxation. I am not going to blame them for making these increases; it seems to me that if they wanted to balance the budget, increases were absolutely essential. And how are they going about these increases? Of the $55,000,000 that they propose to raise, approximately two-thirds will come out of taxation of the necessaries of life by way of an increase in the sales tax or by a two per cent increase in the excise duties. I do not disapprove, in fact I approve of the action of the government in increasing the income tax. I realize that if they had to balance the budget, they have taken, under the system which now prevails in this country, the only logical course which it was possible for them to take-that of increasing the income tax. It was stated by the Minister of Finance when he introduced the budget that, with one exception, he did not intend to make changes in the tariff structure of the country. I think that there was one very important change in the tariff, however, and that was when he increased the excise duty from one to three per cent. I regard that as a very fundamental change in the whole tariff structure of the country, because an increase from one to three per cent means, on the average, roughly speaking, an increase of about ten per cent in all protective duties in Canada. In 1922, when the Liberal party were in power, they found themselves in somewhat the same position as the present government now find themselves in, and they resorted to almost the identical methods which the Conservative party are adopting to-day; that is to say, they increased the sales tax to six per cent. It is quite true that subsequently it was reduced until it reached a level of about one and a half or two per cent, but now we find the sales tax back at the figure it was about ten years ago.
If capitalism demands a balanced budget, then I say that there is practically no alternative to what has been done by the
government on the present occasion. To me, however, the only other alternative is to make a complete break with the existing economic system. But in this house we find very little desire on either side to break with the system. What do we find further? We find that the government, in following out the policy of curtailment in expenditures in the attempt to balance the budget, are merely following the dictates of the financial interests of the country. I go a little further and say that parliament finds itself under the nominal control of those institutions which control the finances of this and other countries of the world. Our municipalities, our legislatures and even this parliament can hardly move without their consent. Our provincial governments find themselves more or less at the behest of the financial institutions; they are being told to balance their budgets, otherwise they will not be permitted to do any more financing.
Where does the real power lie? Does it lie inside of parliament or in the hands of a comparative few outside? We boast of our democratic institutions; perhaps we have good reason to do so, but they are being successfully challenged by those who own and control finance. We claim that we are living under a form of democracy, but I contend that we are living under a form of political democracy which exists side by side with a financial autocracy; in other words, we are half a democracy and half an autocracy. These two forms of government cannot continue to go on indefinitely side by side; sooner or later one must give way to the other. I think it was Lincoln who said during the civil war in the United States that that country could not exist half free and half enslaved. We cannot exist in this country one half a democracy and one half a dictatorship; the one must ultimately give way to the other. I am satisfied that when democracy comes to grips with financial autocracy there can be only one ultimate end to the struggle.
I come now to some of the desires expressed by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) and I shall deal with some aspects of the social question. We have been told that we are suffering from certain financial difficulties. At various times during the present session hon. members have discussed the fact that in this country' we have too much coal. Other hon. members have told us that we have too much fish. We have been told we have too much wheat, too much meat, a surplus of railway equipment and too many railway's. On another occasion we were told there were too many doctors; we have been
191S
The Budget-Mr. Heaps

prevailing economic conditions. What hope is
the government bolding out to those who at present find -themselves out of work? The Minister of Trade and Commerce waxed eloquent when he was pointing out that world conditions are to an extent responsible for our internal situation. In a sense it may be quite true that to-day no nation can live entirely unto itself. But may I put this question to the minister and the house: Is it logical for one to assume that because we cannot sell our wheat and other food products to Great Britain, China, Japan, France, Germany, Roumania and other countries, if all these other countries are too poor to buy the products which we have in superabundance, is that any escuse for our people going hungry and barefooted? If our elevators are crammed with foodstuffs, and the people of China, Japan and the other countries I have mentioned are unable to purchase them, is it logical for us to assume or to say that we should deny those commodities to our own people in Canada who are producing them with the sweat of their own labour? These are facts to which hon. members might give their attention, and if a committee of the house had been set u-p to.deal with them I think both the house and the country would have received more advantage than they have from the efforts of the committees I have just enumerated.
We are told again and again that conditions are bad in the United States. I am quite ready to admit they are bad, but poverty and chaos in the United States are no excuse for a similar condition in this country. Even though world conditions may to some extent be responsible for internal conditions in Canada, the government responsible for the affairs of the nation must accept responsibility for conditions in our midst. I resent very much being told constantly about what is happening in the United States. While I may have a great deal of respect for some activities south of the boundary line I am not one who is always anxious to go to the United States -for illustrations of what we should do.
I am reminded of a statement made a few days ago by a well known English economist who told of the impressions he had received upon a trip to the United States. He said that in that country people were losing faith in institutions and in public men. I hope this government will not ask us to follow the example of a country in which conditions of that kind prevail. This afternoon at the close of the speech by the hon. member for Shel-[DOT]burne-Yarmouth and the peroration of the

Minister of Trade and Commerce, fine language was used and great heights of oratory attained. They were most eloquent as to what conditions should obtain, but not as to ho-w those conditions were to be brought about. I remember some of the expressions used by each hon. member. From the Liberal side of the house we heard the statement that they desired a removal of the restrictions on commerce and a freer interchange of commodities. Mr. Speaker, anything that removes artificial barriers between nation and nation so as to allow a freer flow of commerce has, gen&r-ally speaking, my approval. But we must have something more than that. Free interchange of commodities is one thing, but the great masses of the people should have freer access to the commodities which are produced. Free exchange of commerce is one thing, but it is another thing to have a fairer distribution of products. Unless we have a more equitable distribution of wealth, in my humible opinion there is no hope of solving our economic problems. Again, in my opinion the solution of our difficulties is not to be found exclusively in either raising or lowering tariff barriers. May I here interpose this remark: If those who attend the Imperial economic conference in July next believe that by a process of tariff barriers or tariff adjustments they will bring about a state of prosperity, we must expect a certain amount of disappointment. So far any efforts to bring about a state of prosperity by tariff adjustments within the empire have proved more or less disastrous to the Dominion of Canada. I refer to trade treaties made by the previous and present governments between this country and Australia and New Zealand. An illustration of what may happen is to be found in the despatches appearing in this morning's papers. One of the Australian delegates has stated that the empire will be disrupted if some satisfactory tariff adjustments are not made between its various component parts. It is my firm belief that closer relationships within the empire cannot be brought about by a .process of tariffs. Trade flowed more freely in the years 1928 and 1929 than it flows to-day. In those years we had unemployment; vast numbers of men and women were seeking -work. Restrictions in those years were not as high as they are to-day, and yet at that time we had exactly the same fundamental principles to deal with as we have now. We had wealth on the one hand and poverty on the other. In spite of the fact that we have somewhat changed our fiscal policy, prosperity has not returned to us.

The Budget-Mr. MacNicol
While hon. members in this corner of the house welcomed some of the statements made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, we must say that up to the present time the actions of the government have not given us very much encouragement; they have not held out any hope of dealing effectively with the problem of unemployment. So far their efforts to adjust the tariff have been more or less a failure, and I sincerely hope the statement made this afternoon by the minister to the effect that we should study these social questions is not addressed to hon. members in this comer of the house but to his colleagues in the cabinet. I trust he is asking them to deal with these fundamental problems.
The minister referred to the crushing burden of our national debt. May I point out that in 1914 the interest charges on that debt amounted to 8-5 per cent of the national revenue? In 1932, according to the figures submitted by the Minister of Finance, the interest on our national debt has increased to 8135.000,000 per year-in other words, from 8-5 per cent to 35-6 per cent of the national revenue. It is this crushing burden which is preventing our return to more normal times. One way to bring about the conditions the minister desires is to tackle that problem and see that our interest charges are restored to the position of 1914.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in this debate I propose
to base my remarks on the fact that in its budget for 1932 the government has maintained intact the tariff enactments of the budgets of the short session of 1930 and the regular session of 1931. During the recess, to ascertain the extent of stimulation in industry brought about as a result of tariff enactments, I made a survey of employment in industry in many Canadian centres and in several of the neighbouring states, in the latter to derive firsthand information concerning the effects if any, of the Bennett tariff on American industry. It is my purpose to submit data showing that in spite of worldwide economic dislocation, employment in Canada, although below normal, is better than it would have been had it not been for the tariff enactments of this government. Four of the major objectives sought to be attained by budget legislation with respect to the stimulation of employment in industry are, first, more jobs for Canadian workers; second, greater purchasing power; third, contentment; fourth, increasing
to the greatest possible extent towards 100 per cent the Canadian content, both material and labour, in goods manufactured in Canadian factories by Canadians for Canadians.
In spite of the present worldwide economic dislocation the government has achieved something worth while towards the realization of each of these objectives. The Toronto Industrial Commission has issued a circular stating that since August, 1930, some sixty-seven new industries, mostly small, have been started in the Toronto district, and Industrial Canada and the Bureau of Statistics give the names of fifty-two other companies, mostly small but a few are large, that have been started throughout the country. I know most of these industries are small, and consequently the pay-roll is not heavy; on the other hand the increased employment in the aggregate is considerable. The large majority of these new industries have come from the United States; a few of the largest are of British origin. But, large or small, the figures pertaining to these new organizations are in my humble opinion worth consideration, and I have carefully tabulated them. These new industries occupy a floor space of 4,095,000 square feet; the capital invested in them amounts to $34,125,000; the Canadian content of material and labour-mostly labour- is sixty-seven per cent; the number of employees, 8,950. Anyone acquainted with industry knows that for every man or woman engaged in any manufacturing plant another employee is engaged outside providing the raw material and the one thousand and one articles that enter that industry through the receiving office. So in addition to the 8,950 men engaged in these 119 new factory branches, it may be taken for granted that another 8,950 workers are engaged outside. But as many of these new plants are branches of United States concerns, I will place the additional number engaged outside at 50 per cent or 4,475, so as to foe well within the mark. I submit that that is something to be proud of.
In addition to that a further considerable amount of employment has been provided existing Canadian factories producing goods for the Canadian customers of United States companies, goods that now cannot be shipped in here owing to the tariff regulations made by this government. Thereby employment is provided in Canada for Canadian workmen that otherwise would be provided for the workmen of the United States. Let me give a number of instances of individual plants. The John T. Hepburn Company, Toronto, has invested many thousands of dollars in

The Budget-Mr. MacNicol

equipment for the manufacture of goods hitherto made by American firms. The president told me that twenty-five per cent of their men are now engaged in making goods for Canadians that were formerly made in foreign plants by foreign workmen. The Gray Forgings and Tool Company is another concern that has invested many thousands of dollars in machinery to turn out a complete line of tools for motor cars, and to-day they are making a set of forged wrenches that hitherto were not made in this country, but were imported from Massachusetts and Connecticut. Those two plants are located in the riding which I have the honour to represent. Then I might cite the Canadian General Electric Company-a very large concern-the Gold Medal Furniture Company, the Easy Washing Machine Company, the Canadian National Carbon Company, the Patons & Baldwin Textile Company, the Hamilton Gear and Machine Company; all these companies are manufacturing goods not hitherto made in Canada, and which would still continue to be made in foreign plants were it not for the tariff regulations enacted by the government in 1930 and 1931. The Corman Engineering Company, Toronto, one of several small companies, make a long line of repair parts for foreign machines, parts that formerly we had to import. This company during the last nine months have had twenty-two machinists working full time, and on three days of the week they run two shifts. In addition to repair parts they make a variety of new equipment not hitherto manufactured in Canada, and which but for the present tariff regulations would now be imported to the disadvantage of Canadian labour. The management of the company told me that fifty per cent of their employees are now engaged in making equipment that otherwise would be made across the line. In addition there are twenty-two men outside the company engaged in making the brass and iron castings and the long line of equipment used by the company.
In south Toronto there is a large boiler and engine works, and in east Toronto there is a large link belt factory; I refer to only these two of the many in Toronto which I could mention. Both these companies are making asphalt plants. I will not discuss that item further at the moment because I will come back to it later in connection with another firm. The manager of the boiler and engine factory told me recently that sixty per cent of the men engaged in that industry are making equipment which, but for the tariff enacted by this government, would be made by foreign
EMr. MacNicol.]
workmen in foreign plants and shipped to this country.	.
Now let us go outside Toronto, to one or two other industrial centres. In the city of Brantford there is another large boiler and engine works, which also makes large asphalt plants for a company in Milwaukee. These plants are very large and are worth approximately $30,000 each, while the labour content built into each one is the equivalent of three thousand man-days. I am told that five of.these machines have been made in Canada already. In other words, as a result of the tariff enacted by this government, in those five machines alone fifteen thousand man-days have been gained to labour in Canada.
In Dundas I visited a very large plant of which every Canadian might well be proud, and just here I might say that in discussing these matters with the heads of these different companies the talk was about employment and entirely non-,poliitical; I did not want politics to be dragged into my discussions with those gentlemen. The plant to which I refer is one of the largest, if not the largest, of its kind on the north half of this continent, and there I found Canadian workmen making four lines of large machinery for mines, oil wells and so on. To give hon. members some conception of the size of one of those machines, the day I visited the plant the machinists of the company were lathing a forging made in Welland, Ontario, the largest ever made in Canada. It was a shaft for a hoist, and the finished article weighed seventeen tons. Fancy the size of the completed hoist for which the shaft was made; I may tell the house that it weighs 135 tons and will lift 12,000 pounds from the bottom of a mine 4,000 feet deep. That equipment is a credit to Canadian management, Canadian workmen and Canadian industry, and it demonstrates what Canadian industry can do when it is given a chance. Those four lines of equipment are giving employment to many men who otherwise would not be employed; thousands of man-days enter into the construction of each machine.
Now for a short time I will pass from individual factories to groups of factories, and I will commence with the washing machine industry. The tariff enacted in the spring of 1930 by the previous government reduced the duty on washing machine parts to 10 per cent, and made the whole industry in Canada merely an assembling proposition. The present government raised the duty to 35 per cent and the result has been romantic, if one may use that word in speaking of business. What has been the result? Thirty thousand tubs, the clothes part of the washing machine, either of nickel

The Budget-Mr. MacNicol
plated capper or enamelled steel, which formerly came from Warren, Ohio, are now made in London, Ontario; twenty thousand clothes wringers formerly made in Erie, Pennsylvania, and Woonsocket, Rhode Island, are now made by Canadians at St. Mary's, at Hamilton, at Toronto, at Farnham and other Canadian centres. Thirty thousand gear sets and twenty or thirty odd lines that enter into the construction of washing machines are now made in Canadian plants by Canadians, providing 250 new jobs, where formerly they were made in foreign lands by foreign workmen. I say, Mr. Speaker, that is something of which any government can be proud.
Take the printing industry. I have here a list of forty-seven United States magazines now being printed in Canada, and what has been the result? The printing plants of Canada to-day use from 175 to 200 tons of Canadian paper monthly to print these magazines, and that paper is worth from 812,000 to $15,000 a month. The postage and express in connection with the -mailing of these magazines is estimated at another $5,000 a month. The ink used is worth $1,700 a month, and better still 175 new jobs were provided for Canadians in the printing industry, and those 175 Canadians receive $25,000 a month. The publishers belli me that the whole new business adds to the national wealth of Canada about $1,000,000 a year. I say that is something worth while, and something of which we should be proud.
Now take ithe electrical line, covering a great number of plants. During the last two years electrical plants in Canada have invested $2,000,000 in order to equip themselves for -the manufacture of a long line of material formerly imported. In Canada we now make motors ranging in size from one as bag as a ten cent piece, such as operates yonder clock, to one of 54,000 kilowatts or 75,000 horse power. Large sums of money have been invested in equipment necessary to manufacture several new series of motors such as used in house appliances, washing machines, vacuum cleaners and so on, hitherto made in Ithe United states. A complete line of switches is now made here, ranging in size from the small wall push button to the great circuit breakers that automatically cut out a current of 75,000 horse power, or any one of half a dozen generators of 75,000 horse power. Canadian emplayers and Canadian workmen have demonstrated that given the chance they can turn out finished articles to equal anything made anywhere in the world. To-day the electrical business in Montreal, in Toronto, in Peterborough, in Hamilton, in Brantford, in 41761-1211
St. Catharines and in other places is employing 750 men who, if it were not for the tariff regulations enacted by this government since coming into office, would be unemployed.
Now I pass to the steel industry, the steel manufacturers and the steel workers, because you cannot separate one from the other. What is good for the industry is good for the employee, and what is good for the employee is good for ithe industry. The steel industry has benefited very materially by the tariff enactments of this government. In Hamilton a new school of commerce building is l^eing erected. When I saw it, it was half up, and in the framework of that building 970 tons of steel are -being used. Thanks to the patriotic fervour-for in my humble opinion it is nothing less-of the Hamilton board of education, the architects, the engineers, the steel manufacturers and steel fabricators, every ton of -that 970 tons being used in the High School of Commerce is being made in Canada by Canadians, and had it not been for the tariff enactments of this government, perhaps not a ton of Canadian steel would have been used therein. A -new hydro electric building is being erected in Toronto, and 1,000 tons of steel to be used in that building are to be made in Canada by Canadians. A viaduct is being erected in the city of Sarnia, and in that construction there will be 300 tons of steel made in Canada by Canadians. These three jobs have given the Canadian steelworkers 25,000 extra man days which they might not have had had it not been for the tariff enactments of 'this government.
The making of steel is one line which adds to the national wealth and which benefits labour to a very marked degree, because about eighty per cent of a ton of steel represents labour. We are now making steel ingots in Canada, from which steel plate is made, representing from eighty to ninety-five per cent Canadian content. Plates, from a quarter of an inch thick and up to 78 inches wide, are made from ingots of ninety-five per cent Canadian content. In other words, for every hundred dollars' worth of these steel ingots used in the making of plates ninety-five dollars are added to the national wealth, because the money which is paid out is circulated in and remains in Canada. On the other hand, when we send fifty dollars out of Canada to bring in steel plate, nothing is added to the national wealth. I am quite aware, of course, that in addition to that fifty dollars sent out of Canada to bring steel in, there is an additional fifty dollars spent in Canada to finish the product; but that fifty dollars spent on
The Budget-Mr. MacNicol

labour in Canada merely offsets the fifty dollars sent out, so that in reality nothing is added to the national wealth.
There are a number of steel buildings projected at the' present time, and my sincere hope is that public bodies having control of these projects, whether church boards or school boards or other boards, and architects and engineers, observing the great benefit that accrues to the country from the use of steel made by Canadians, will specify flat that the steel to be used in the structures under their control shall be if at all posable made in Canada. In Canada riveted steel girders and uprights are made out of plate and channel iron and angle iron. I am quite aware that in the United States they use H-beams and I-ibeams, but they did not begin the use of these beams there until they had passed the one hundred million mark in population. We Canadians have to look out for ourselves. There are only ten millions of us, and, in my humble opinion, sound tariff legislation that encourages the manufacture of steel plate, angles and girders in Canada, goes a long way towards increasing the national wealth.
My time is going, and forty minutes is hardly long enough to tell even one-fourth of the achievements of this government towards providing employment since it came into office. I have surveyed the textile and leather industries, both of which are running from 90 to 100 per cent, but I do not propose to discuss either of them except to say this in regard to the textile industry. There are at present engaged in Canada in the textile factories 109,575 operators, and the authorities in the textile industry inform me that were it not for the tariff legislation of this government in connection with textiles, one-third less would be employed therein. In other words, this government, as the result of tariff enactments in favour of Canadian employment, in the textile industry, deserves direct credit in that one industry alone for the present employment of over 36,000 operators. Will anyone say that the emplojunent of 36,000 operators is nothing? I do not for a moment try to argue that business is as good as we should like to have it; it is not. I do not think that conditions are as good as we would like, but they are a lot better than they would have been had it not been for the tariff enactments of this government.
The March issue of Industrial Canada gives a list of some 628 new limes, of material manufactured in this country since this government came into power. I am well aware that a great number of these are very small items, but added together they make an. aggregate 
which is commendable. The government deserves credit for encouraging the manufacture of new lines, and in the total employment in this country, according to our own Bureau of Statistics, there are about 900,000 or more engaged in industry at the present time either wholly or part time. I thought I would make a survey to ascertain the value of part time employment, and I obtained the figures from 125 cross-Canada firms all nationally known. Of the 125, sixty-nine replied to my questionnaire, and of that 69, nineteen had no part time employees. I gave them two dates, asking for part time employment on March 1, 1931, and part time employment on May 15, 1931, because I wanted to make a comparison with a similar survey made in Washington, to which I shall allude in a moment. In Canada on March 1, 1931, the part time employment in the balance of these Canadian industries was 30.18 per cent and on May 15 of the same year it was 30.54-very little change. The part time results in the United States were by no means equal to that. In Washington a circular letter was sent out to 750 crosscountry United States firms of which 250 replied, and the part time employment in the United States on March 1, 1931, was 33.5 and on May 15, 1931, 40 per cent. That clearly shows the superiority of Canada and bears out the statement we so often read and hear that conditions are better in this country.
Someone asked some days ago about the number of plants in Canada that had closed since this government came into power. The July, 1931, issue of Industrial Canada contains the advertisements of 340 cross-Canada concerns, and I am very happy to say that as far as I can ascertain everyone of those firms is to-day doing business in Canada. That speaks volumes for the integrity and business ability of Canadian managers and speaks well for the workmen in the plants.
During the course of this debate someone has suggested that nothing has been offered for the improvement of conditions in Canada.
I suggest to the government that practical and technical cost accountants, men conversant with industry be delegated to survey the imports coming into this country. After they have compiled their statistics and presented them to the government, it could then determine what could be economically manufactured in this country with a view to increasing employment and at the same time preventing the exploitation of the consumer. It is not a difficult matter for any government to prevent the exploitation of the consumer. If industry were treated scientifically

Privilege-Mr. Pouliot
and considered with a view to the natural resources of a district, its topography and geology, its climatic conditions, its proximity to water or other transportation facilities for the handling of raw and finished products, and its proximity to markets, power and labour supply, I am firmly convinced that millions of dollars could be invested in this country in the erection of new plants to provide increased employment.
It is the duty of the government in power to create employment if possible. The investment of capital, the extension of existing industries and the building up of new industries creates more and more jobs. Considering the economic dislocation and the distress which exists in the world to-day, the government of this country has done a great deal to provide employment for Canadians. I know of no better way to provide employment than by the erection and operation of factories. Having been associated so 'long with the business life of this country, I know full well that men working in industiy and receiving fair wages are contented and happy. There is no other way to encourage the erection of factories and the investment of capital than by adequate tariff regulations. I take this opportunity to congratulate the government for maintaining in the budget of 1932 the tariff regulations adopted in the budgets of 1930 and 1931 which resulted in so many additional man-days' employment.
During the years 1926, 1927, 1928 and 1929 this country imported $40,000,000 worth of steel plate and structural steel-I do not refer to rolled steel-and had one-half of this been manufactured in Canada by Canadian steel makers it would have given them an additional 3,600,000 man-days' employment. I suggest to the government: maintain the fiscal policy adopted in 1930-31 and proceed along similar lines with future budgets. The result will be most beneficial to employment in this country.
